title: From Nalli Nihari to Lotus Mithais: How Delhi Is Feeding the BRICS Summit
excerpt: The Taj Mahal, New Delhi spent months researching delegate preferences to build an 'India Friendship Menu' for the 18th BRICS Summit — and every delegate goes home with a recipe book.
body:
• The Taj Mahal, New Delhi has spent up to six months researching delegate preferences to curate menus for the 18th BRICS Summit, being held in the capital on September 12-13.
  • Executive Chef Kaushik Misra created an "India Friendship Menu" for in-room dining, featuring Delhi classics like Nalli Nihari and pepper fry with almonds, alongside dishes from across the country.
  • Pralines, mithais and savouries take inspiration from the lotus and orchids — floral symbols in several delegate countries — while a culinary map of India showcases regional specialities state by state.
  • Each delegate will take home a recipe book of chef-curated recipes, including family recipes of the chefs' mothers, as a keepsake of the summit.

As New Delhi hosts the 18th BRICS Summit on September 12 and 13, some of the most meaningful conversations between world leaders may not happen in the conference rooms at all, but around the dining table. The Taj Mahal, New Delhi — the landmark hotel hosting summit delegates — has spent months translating India's identity into food, and the result is one of the most elaborate culinary operations ever mounted for a diplomatic gathering in the capital.

At the centre of the effort is Executive Chef Kaushik Misra, whose team has been researching delegate preferences for between three and six months. The menu is not simply a showcase of Indian cuisine; it is an exercise in what the chef describes as food as a language of friendship, blending regional Indian flavours with comfort-food references from each participating country's own culinary traditions.

The "India Friendship Menu"

The anchor of the operation is an "India Friendship Menu" designed specifically for in-room dining. It brings together classics associated with Delhi and other parts of India — dishes Misra named include Nalli Nihari, the slow-cooked shank stew that is a defining dish of Old Delhi's Mughal-era kitchens, and a pepper fry with almonds, among other curated offerings.

Misra said the concept was built around both India's regional flavours and the familiar tastes of the visitors. "It has been conceptualised keeping in mind various flavours of our own country: the spices, the herbs, the flowers," he told ANI, adding that the team had studied each delegation's likes and dislikes so that "flavours, Indian and theirs, can be experienced here."

"It's been a lot of work by the team, and we have put together everything in a very extensive format so flavours, Indian and theirs, can be experienced here. I am very excited, and we are very confident that we can definitely be able to create memories."

— Kaushik Misra, Executive Chef, Taj Mahal, New Delhi

Flowers, Maps and Edible Symbolism

Beyond the main menu, the hotel's chefs have turned ingredients and flowers into design elements. Pralines, mithais and savouries draw inspiration from the lotus and orchids — floral symbols with significance in several delegate countries — transforming those references into edible forms.

One of the more distinctive creations is a culinary map of India, designed to introduce delegates to the country's geographical and gastronomic diversity. The map pairs references to different capitals and states with the regional savouries of each area — kaju mithai among them — so that the geography of the meal becomes an education in itself. A written concept note accompanies the food, explaining the thinking behind each offering and the significance of the ingredients chosen.

That educational intent is deliberate. For delegates from Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE — the eleven-member grouping that collectively accounts for nearly half the world's population — the meal doubles as an introduction to how regionally varied Indian food actually is.

A Recipe Book to Take Home

Perhaps the most personal touch has nothing to do with what is served at the table. According to Misra, each delegate will receive a recipe book containing chef-curated recipes — including recipes from the chefs' own mothers — intended as a keepsake that travels home after the summit.

The gesture turns hospitality into something portable: a conversation starter and a memory that outlasts the two-day gathering. The book, much like the "India Friendship Menu," frames food as cultural exchange rather than mere catering.

Why Food Diplomacy Matters Here

Indian state hospitality has long used cuisine as a soft-power instrument, and this year's summit — held under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" — arrives at a moment when New Delhi is positioning itself as a bridge-builder for the Global South. The kitchen, in that context, is doing diplomatic work of its own.

For the Indian diaspora watching from abroad, the summit's culinary showcase is also a reminder of how far Indian food has travelled. Dishes that were once described to foreign audiences in simplified terms are now being presented in their full regional complexity — nihari from Old Delhi's lanes, mithais reimagined through floral symbolism — to the leaders of eleven countries at once.

What Comes Next

The summit runs through September 13, with development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges on the agenda. The delegations will return home with briefing documents, communiqués — and, this time, a book of family recipes from a Delhi kitchen. In a gathering defined by declarations, the most enduring souvenir may be the one they can cook.
